couteau.resume: Using a knife safely, carving a feather stick, sawing, and the essential knots.

p: A good bivouac knife has a fixed or securely locking blade of 8 to 10 cm, strong and easy to sharpen. A multi-tool with a small saw complements it very well. In Belgium as elsewhere, a knife is carried stowed away (in the pack or its sheath) and only for a justified use such as bivouacking.

liste: Always cut with the blade moving away from you.
The “blood circle”: before cutting, stretch out your arm holding the closed knife and turn around. Nobody should be inside that circle.
Work sitting down, elbows on knees, blade outside your thighs (the femoral artery runs on the inside).
Never cut towards the hand holding the wood.
Close or put away the knife as soon as you stop using it.
A sharp knife is safer than a blunt one, which slips and makes you force it.

p: The king of techniques for lighting a fire in wet weather: you turn a dead stick into a tuft of dry curls that catch easily.
etapes: Choose a dead stick as thick as a thumb, and split it to reach the dry heartwood.
Rest the end of the stick on a stump or log, angled at about 45°.
Lay the blade flat against the wood and push it down in long, very thin curls.
Stop each curl just before the base so it stays attached.
Make 10 to 20 curls, turning the stick: you get a “feather” ready to take a spark.

liste: A folding saw is safer and more effective than an axe for bivouac wood.
To split a log with a knife (“batoning”): place the blade on the end of the upright log and strike the back of the blade with another stick. Only with a strong fixed-blade knife.
Never cut living wood: it doesn't burn and it is forbidden.

p: Without rope, nature provides: long nettle stems and the inner bark of the lime tree give strong fibres. They are combined by “reverse twisting”: two strands each twisted towards you then crossed away from you. The result holds surprisingly well for tying, lashing or hanging.
Five knots cover almost every bivouac need. Their detailed sheets, with photos, are in the Knots category.
liste: The bowline: a fixed loop that doesn't slip.
Round turn and two half hitches: tying a rope to a tree.
The trucker's hitch: tensioning a ridgeline very tightly.
The taut-line hitch: adjusting the tension of the tarp's guylines.
The Prusik: an attachment point that slides on a taut rope.

hygiene.resume: Looking after your feet, hands and health during several days outdoors.

p: Damaged feet turn a trip into an ordeal, and in a survival situation they can stop you reaching help.
liste: Keep your feet dry: change socks as soon as they're wet, dry the damp pair on you or in the sun.
Treat hot spots BEFORE they become blisters.
In the evening, wash, dry and air your feet, and check for blisters and ticks.
Cut your toenails short before you go.

Feet that are wet and cold for hours, several days in a row, can develop “immersion foot” (white, swollen, numb and then painful feet). Dry and warm them every evening, and see a doctor if feeling doesn't come back.
Wash your hands after the toilet and before eating: most bivouac diarrhoea comes from hands, not water.
Brush your teeth with boiled or filtered water, spit far from water sources.
Wash with a flannel or biodegradable wipe, soap away from the river.
Keep a clean, dry outfit for the night.

etapes: Go more than 50 m from water, camp and paths.
Dig a hole 15 to 20 cm deep with a small trowel or a stick.
Fill it in carefully and put leaves or moss back on top.
Take the toilet paper away in a sealed bag: it takes months to disappear.

liste: Ticks: full check every evening (armpits, groin, behind the knees, scalp), removal with a tick remover.
Mosquitoes and horseflies: long clothing at dusk, repellent.
Processionary caterpillars: don't camp under infested trees.
Nettle, giant hogweed: know the plants that sting or burn.
Plasters of various sizes, blister plasters, dressings, bandage, tape
Disinfectant, hand gel
Tick remover, tweezers, small scissors
Painkillers, personal medicines
Survival blanket, disposable gloves
Emergency numbers (in Bivaska: SOS button and Poisoning sheet)

secours_guide.resume: Calling for help, giving your position, making yourself visible and guiding a helicopter.

etapes: Dial 112: it works throughout Europe, and goes through any available mobile network.
Say who you are, what is happening, how many people are involved and their condition.
Give your GPS position (Bivaska's SOS button: coordinates to read out or copy).
Don't hang up first, and keep the phone switched on afterwards.

encadre.texte: If the call doesn't go through, an SMS sometimes gets through where voice fails. Climbing higher also improves signal.

liste: Aeroplane mode between attempts, brightness at minimum.
Power bank kept warm in an inside pocket (cold drains batteries).
Agree a switch-on time with the rescuers if you're in contact.
Anything in threes means distress: 3 whistle blasts, 3 flashes of light, 3 fires in a triangle.
On the ground, in a clearing: a large V (need help) or X (need medical assistance), at least 4 × 6 m, with strokes 1 m wide, in branches, stones or high-contrast clothing.
A brightly coloured garment or survival blanket, spread out in an open place.
A mirror or the phone screen to flash the sun at a plane or helicopter.
By day, white smoke (green leaves on the fire); at night, a bright flame or the head torch.
Signal with both arms raised in a Y towards the sky: “yes, need help”. One arm raised, the other lowered: “no, no need”.
Tie down or put away anything that could blow away (tarp, bags, survival blanket).
Never approach the aircraft without a sign from the crew, and always from the front, in the pilot's field of view.

loi.titre: Law and ethics, country by country
loi.resume: Where are you allowed to sleep, light a fire, forage? The rules in Belgium, France, Switzerland, Germany, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.

p: In all these countries, the basic rule is the same: you can't camp just anywhere. Bivouacking (a single night, evening to morning, without setting up camp) is sometimes tolerated where camping is forbidden. Nature reserves, national parks and private land always have their own rules. This information is a summary: always check the local rules before you go.

liste: Wallonia: camping in the forest is forbidden, except in designated bivouac areas (shown on Bivaska's map when they are listed) or on private land with the owner's permission.
Flanders: only in the designated bivouac zones.
Fire: forbidden in forests, except at designated spots.
Foraging: generally tolerated in small quantities for personal use, unless locally banned; forbidden in nature reserves; owner's permission on private land.
Bivouacking is allowed where it isn't forbidden. Frequent bans: listed and protected sites, the seashore, around drinking-water catchments, public roads, private land without permission.
National parks: each has its own rules. Some allow bivouacking at set times (often 7 pm to 9 am) or near mountain huts, others ban it completely (Port-Cros, Calanques).
Fire: forbidden in woods and within 200 m of them for anyone who isn't the owner, with stricter bans in summer.
Wild camping isn't banned by federal law, but cantons and municipalities set the rules, which are often restrictive.
Above the tree line, one night in a small tent, not in a group, is generally tolerated.
Forbidden in nature reserves, the Swiss National Park, federal game reserves and wildlife quiet zones.
No single rule: each Land decides. Camping in the forest almost everywhere requires the permission of the owner or the forestry authority.
Sleeping under the stars for one night, without a tent (“Biwak”), is often tolerated outside protected areas.
Some regions offer official bivouac pitches (Trekkingplätze), to be booked.
Netherlands: wild camping is forbidden. You sleep at “paalkampeerplaatsen”, free and basic bivouac pitches in the forest.
Luxembourg: considered generally forbidden outside campsites; on private land, the owner's permission is required.
Take all your rubbish away, including food waste.
Stay discreet: arrive late, leave early, no music, small groups.
Respect wildlife: don't feed, don't approach, dogs on a lead.
Forage in moderation, never protected species.
Leave the place cleaner than you found it.

encadre.texte: Every badly kept bivouac gets one more place closed. Bivouacking stays tolerated as long as it stays invisible.

secourisme.titre: First aid, alone and far from everything
secourisme.resume: When help won't come quickly, or at all: stabilise, protect from the cold, monitor, then decide whether to stay or go.

p: In town, first aid is about holding on for a few minutes. Far from everything, without signal, you may have to look after a casualty, or yourself, for hours or days. The goal is no longer to wait for the ambulance: it is to stabilise, prevent things getting worse, and choose the right moment to get out.
Even without signal, still try to raise the alarm: climb to a high point, send an SMS to a loved one with your position, prepare distress signals (Signals sheet).

etapes: Danger: remove whatever still threatens (falling rocks, water, fire), without putting yourself in danger.
Heavy bleeding: stop it immediately (pressure, tourniquet if needed).
Breathing: open the airway, recovery position if the person is unconscious and breathing.
Cold: insulate from the ground, cover, shelter. A casualty who isn't moving cools down very quickly, even in summer.
Everything else next: fractures, wounds, pain, drinking.

liste: Stay and signal if: the casualty can't walk or can't be left alone, night or bad weather is coming, the way is unknown, or someone knows where you are and is expecting you.
Go if: nobody will look for you, the casualty can walk safely or can be left stable and sheltered, and you know the way to somewhere you can call from.
A casualty who can still walk should move slowly, with a lightened pack, by the safest route, not the shortest.

sections.titre: Signs that mean getting out fast
liste: Consciousness drops or the person becomes confused.
They have trouble breathing.
Bleeding won't stop, or a tourniquet has been applied.
Pallor, cold sweats, fast pulse: shock.
Increasing belly pain, repeated vomiting.
A wound becomes infected (spreading redness, fever).
Hypothermia: shivering that stops, clumsy movements, incoherent speech.

encadre.titre: Just one of these signs is enough
encadre.texte: As soon as one of these signs appears, waiting becomes more dangerous than the effort: do everything to evacuate or be found.

p: Every hour, note the casualty's condition: consciousness, breathing, pulse, skin, pain. A change shows in the notes long before you can see it. The sheet Monitoring a casualty explains how.

liste: A tourniquet and dressings, a compression bandage
Strips (adhesive sutures) and plasters
Fine tweezers and a tick remover
Something to rinse a wound (syringe or bottle with a pierced cap)
A survival blanket and gloves
Painkillers and antihistamines, your adrenaline pen if you are allergic
A notebook and a pencil

encadre.texte: First-aid training, and if possible a “remote environment” module, is worth more than the best kit.
